Replacing worn turf in Poinciana's earliest villages

A full tear-out and relay in Poinciana gets priced per job once the crew has opened up the old lawn, not from a flat rate per square foot. The community's original villages date to 1972, and turf put in there anywhere from the early 2010s back is now old enough in places that replacement, rather than another round of spot repair, is the straight answer.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Two growth waves left two different replacement timelines

Turf generally lasts 10 to 20 years depending on UV stabilization, traffic and infill, and Poinciana's oldest conversions cluster around two distinct building waves: the first villages built soon after the 1972 founding, and the larger wave that followed once Avatar Holdings, later AV Homes, took over development in the mid-1980s. A lawn converted early in either wave is closer to the upper end of that service-life range than one converted in a 2000s-era section of the same village, which matters more to a replacement timeline than the house's own age does. Our guide to turf lifespan in Florida covers what shortens that window on a given lot.

The state's material rule is newer than a lot of the turf already down

Rule 62-308.100 didn't take effect until May 2026, which means turf installed in Poinciana any time before that could have gone in over unwashed base material or with an infill the rule wouldn't allow on a new job today. A full replacement is the point where that gets corrected as a matter of course, since the old base and infill come out with the worn turf anyway; there's no separate obligation to retrofit a yard that isn't being touched, but rebuilding to the current standard while the ground is already open costs little extra against putting the same specification back.

A base that looks flat but was never washed to begin with

An older Poinciana lawn's base can appear level and well-compacted on the surface while still holding a fines crust from subgrade material that was never washed before the original install, years before the current standard required it. That crust doesn't announce itself as a problem until the turf above it is pulled up during a replacement, at which point it's clear the base was never actually draining the way it looked like it was. Flat isn't the same as functional, which is why we check for a crust, not just for slope, before deciding a base can stay.

Staging demo so old debris doesn't contaminate a kept base

When part of a Poinciana lawn's base is solid enough to reuse, the old turf and infill coming out of the rest of the yard get staged and hauled away in a way that keeps loose material from falling back into the section being kept. Skipping this staging step risks mixing years-old, possibly crusted infill back into a base that was otherwise fine, undoing the reason for keeping it in the first place. This sequencing matters more on a replacement than a first-time install, since there's old material moving through the site that a new-build job never has to manage.

Say you have a 2011-installed lawn in Village 2

Say you have a lawn converted to turf in 2011 in Village 2, worn thin along the path from the driveway to the back gate and slower to drain than it used to be after a storm. At roughly 15 years in the ground, that lawn is deep into its expected service window, and a replacement quote works out from what the crew finds once the old turf comes up, whether the rock underneath still drains well enough to reuse or has to come out along with everything on top of it.

Choosing a PFAS-free product during a replacement

Florida's turf standard bars intentionally added PFAS in any new synthetic turf installation, and a Poinciana homeowner replacing an older lawn gets to choose from current product lines built to that standard rather than whatever was on the market when the original turf went in. Asking a supplier for documentation on this point during a replacement is a reasonable ask, since it's exactly the kind of material change a full re-turf is positioned to address that a smaller repair job never would be.

Replacement is also when the village board looks again

APV's and Solivita's landscaping criteria treat a full tear-out and relay as an exterior change no different from a first-time install, so a replacement project goes back through the DCB or the ARC even on a lawn that's carried turf for a decade or more already. That second look is also the practical moment to confirm a canal- or pond-adjacent layout against the state's 10-foot waterbody setback, since an install that predates the current rule can sit closer to the water than a new submittal would be approved for today. Our piece on what a turf warranty actually covers is worth reading before assuming a manufacturer's coverage still applies to a lawn this old.

An irrigation line capped with tape instead of properly sealed

A sprinkler line simply folded over and taped rather than cut back and capped with a proper fitting is a common shortcut on a Poinciana replacement, and tape doesn't hold against water pressure the way a sealed cap does. A line that fails this way months later can undermine the new base from below with a slow, hidden leak, the kind of problem that's invisible until a soft spot appears in turf that's only been down a short time. Confirming each line was properly capped, not just covered, is worth asking about directly.

Watching a corrected footprint for a new drainage low point

Moving a Poinciana lawn's edge outside a live oak's drip line or farther back from a setback line during replacement changes where water moves across that section of yard, even when the correction itself was overdue and necessary. The boundary where the new, adjusted footprint meets the older, unchanged part of the lawn is worth watching through the first few storms, since a grade change at that line can create a small low point that wasn't there under the old layout until the new one settles in fully.

Questions people ask

How do I know if Poinciana turf needs replacing instead of repairing?

The condition of the rock underneath, not just how the surface looks, is what decides it. If that base still drains well once probed, a repair on the surface is often enough; if it's crusted over or holding water, replacement is the more honest fix, and the only way to tell for certain is to open up a section and look.

Does a replacement project need DCB or ARC approval again?

Yes. Either board treats a full tear-out and relay as an exterior change no different from new construction, so the same landscaping submittal applies regardless of how long turf was already on the lot.
